```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(dr3)
ok  <- requireNamespace("Hmisc", quietly = TRUE) &&
       requireNamespace("SuperLearner", quietly = TRUE)
rhc <- if (ok) tryCatch(dr_rhc(), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  eval = !is.null(rhc), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center"
)
```

Everything in dr3 works the same way for a **binary** outcome; only the scale of
the answer changes — the average treatment effect becomes a **risk difference**,
`E[Y^1] - E[Y^0]` on the probability scale. We use the right-heart
catheterization (RHC) study of Connors et al. (1996): does placing a
Swan-Ganz catheter within 24h of ICU admission (`swang1`) change 30-day
mortality? It is a real observational dataset, so there is no known truth.

```{r note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = is.null(rhc)}
cat("> This article needs the suggested package **Hmisc** (to download RHC from",
    "the public Vanderbilt repository), **SuperLearner**, and an internet",
    "connection; its code is shown but not run here.\n")
```

## Load the data

`dr_rhc()` downloads Vanderbilt's R-format export of RHC (`rhc.sav`) from the public
Vanderbilt biostatistics repository via `Hmisc::getHdata()` — dr3 ships no data — and
returns the treatment, the binary outcome, and one-hot-encoded covariates.

The paper analyses Vanderbilt's CSV export of the same dataset (`rhc.csv`). The two
exports differ slightly: four factors have different reference levels, and numeric
covariates differ by at most about 5e-6. Estimates from this loader can therefore
differ slightly from the paper's (see `?dr_rhc`), apart from the smaller learner
library used below.

```{r load}
str(rhc[c("name", "outcome_type")])
c(n = length(rhc$Y), treated = sum(rhc$A), deaths = sum(rhc$Y))
```

## One call

`dr_panel()` detects the binary outcome and targets on the risk-difference scale
automatically (the TMLE scaling uses `y_range = c(0, 1)`). Pass
`family_y = binomial()` so the shared Super Learner fits the outcome model as a
probability.

```{r panel}
set.seed(1)   # the full-sample fits use the current RNG state; `seed` sets the folds
fit <- dr_panel(rhc$Y, rhc$A, rhc$X, family_y = binomial(),
                SL.library = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm", "SL.glmnet"), seed = 1)
fit
```

```{r forest}
plot(fit, xlab = "risk difference (30-day mortality)")
```

## Reading the panel

Every doubly-robust estimate is **positive** — RHC is associated with higher
30-day mortality — reproducing the direction of the original Connors et al.
finding. Compare the full-sample rows with the cross-fit ones: in the paper's RHC
analysis (Step 4) the full-sample AIPW read lower than the cross-fit estimates, with
smaller in-sample residuals and a smaller one-step correction than out of fold;
with the small library used here the two are close. Without ground truth, neither
gap would establish which estimate is more accurate. The
singly-robust plug-ins (g-computation, IPTW) carry no analytic interval.

Because the outcome is a 0/1 event, the estimates and their Wald intervals are on
the risk-difference scale: a value of `0.05` means five extra deaths per hundred
patients attributable to catheterization under the no-unmeasured-confounding
assumption.
